==Education and early life==
MacMillan was born in [[Bellshill]], [[North Lanarkshire]], [[Scotland]], in 1968 and grew up in nearby [[New Stevenston]].<ref name="BBC"/> His father was a steelworker, while his grandfather was a miner.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2021 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2021/macmillan/183036-david-macmillan-interview-february-2022/ |access-date=2025-01-04 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US |archive-date=7 October 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241007171350/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2021/macmillan/183036-david-macmillan-interview-february-2022/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He attended the local state-funded schools, New Stevenston Primary and Bellshill Academy, and credited his Scottish education and Scottish upbringing for his success.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Success wouldn't have happened if I wasn't Scottish, says Bellshill-born Nobel Prize winner|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/business_hq/19631329.professor-david-wc-macmillan-success-wouldnt-happened-wasnt-scottish/|access-date=2021-11-09|website=HeraldScotland|date=7 October 2021|language=en|archive-date=9 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211109191423/https://www.heraldscotland.com/business_hq/19631329.professor-david-wc-macmillan-success-wouldnt-happened-wasnt-scottish/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="BBC">{{Cite news|date=7 October 2021|title=David MacMillan: 'Being Scottish helped me win Nobel Prize'|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-58828279|access-date=7 October 2021|archive-date=7 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007101315/https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-58828279|url-status=live}}</ref>

He received his undergraduate degree in chemistry at the [[University of Glasgow]], where he worked with Ernie Colvin.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bellshill man and former Glasgow University student David WC MacMillan wins the Nobel prize for chemistry|url=https://www.glasgowtimes.co.uk/news/19630090.bellshill-man-former-glasgow-university-student-david-wc-macmillan-wins-nobel-prize-chemistry/|access-date=7 October 2021|work=Glasgow Times|archive-date=9 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009190615/https://www.glasgowtimes.co.uk/news/19630090.bellshill-man-former-glasgow-university-student-david-wc-macmillan-wins-nobel-prize-chemistry/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=nas>{{cite web |title=David MacMillan |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/david-macmillan-zfvtlj/ |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |access-date=7 October 2021 |archive-date=24 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324141208/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/20044093.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 1990, he left the UK to begin his doctoral studies under the direction of Professor [[Larry Overman]] at the [[University of California, Irvine]]. During this time, he focused on the development of new reaction methodology directed toward the stereocontrolled formation of bicyclic [[tetrahydrofuran]]s. MacMillan's graduate studies culminated in the total synthesis of {{nowrap|7-(−)-deacetoxyalcyonin}} acetate, a eunicellin [[Terpenoid|diterpenoid]] isolated from the soft coral ''Eunicella stricta''.<ref>{{Cite thesis |title=Stereocontrolled formation of bicyclic tetrahydrofurans; and, Enantioselective total synthesis of eunicellin diterpenes |oclc=35966904 |date=1996 |first=David William Cross |last=MacMillan  |id={{ProQuest|304225710}} |institution=[[University of California, Irvine]] |degree=Ph.D.}}</ref> He earned his Ph.D. in 1996.<ref name=nas/>

==Career and research==
Upon receiving his Ph.D., MacMillan accepted a postdoctoral position with Professor [[David A. Evans|David Evans]] at [[Harvard University]]. His postdoctoral studies centered on enantioselective catalysis, in particular, the design and development of [[Tin|Sn(II)]]-derived [[Bisoxazoline ligand|bisoxazoline]] complexes (Sn(II)box).<ref name=nas />

MacMillan began his independent research career as a member of the chemistry faculty at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in July 1998. He joined the department of chemistry at [[Caltech]] in June 2000, where his group's research interests centered on new approaches to enantioselective catalysis. In 2004, he was appointed as the [[Earle C. Anthony]] Professor of Chemistry. He became the James S. McDonnell Distinguished University Professor at [[Princeton University]] in September 2006.<ref name=nas />

[[File:MacMillan-Catalyst first generation.svg|thumb|First generation MacMillan catalyst]]
He is considered to be one of the founders of [[organocatalysis]].<ref name="Castelvecchi Stoye p. ">{{cite journal | last1=Castelvecchi | first1=Davide | last2=Stoye | first2=Emma | title='Elegant' catalysts that tell left from right scoop chemistry Nobel | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | date=6 October 2021 | volume=598 | issue=7880 | pages=247–248 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/d41586-021-02704-2 | pmid=34616090 | bibcode=2021Natur.598..247C | s2cid=238422185 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Ahrendt Borths MacMillan pp. 4243–4244">{{cite journal | last1=Ahrendt | first1=Kateri A. | last2=Borths | first2=Christopher J. | last3=MacMillan | first3=David W. C. | title=New Strategies for Organic Catalysis: The First Highly Enantioselective Organocatalytic Diels−Alder Reaction | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | publisher=American Chemical Society (ACS) | volume=122 | issue=17 | date=15 April 2000 | issn=0002-7863 | doi=10.1021/ja000092s | pages=4243–4244 | bibcode=2000JAChS.122.4243A }}</ref> MacMillan's research group has made many advances in the field of asymmetric organocatalysis, and they have applied these new methods to the synthesis of a range of complex natural products.<ref name=nas /><ref name="Castelvecchi Stoye p. " /> He developed chiral [[imidazolidinone]] catalysts.<ref name="Princeton University Department of Chemistry 2014">{{cite web | title=David MacMillan | website=Princeton University Department of Chemistry | date=21 July 2014 | url=https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/david-macmillan | access-date=7 October 2021 | archive-date=7 October 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211007050724/https://chemistry.princeton.edu/faculty/david-macmillan | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Ahrendt Borths MacMillan pp. 4243–4244" /><ref name="Paras MacMillan pp. 7894–7895">{{cite journal | last1=Paras | first1=Nick A. | last2=MacMillan | first2=David W. C. | title=The Enantioselective Organocatalytic 1,4-Addition of Electron-Rich Benzenes to α,β-Unsaturated Aldehydes | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | publisher=American Chemical Society (ACS) | volume=124 | issue=27 | date=12 June 2002 | issn=0002-7863 | doi=10.1021/ja025981p | pages=7894–7895| pmid=12095321 | bibcode=2002JAChS.124.7894P | url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20170414-104130125 }}</ref> {{ill|MacMillan catalysts|de|MacMillan-Katalysatoren}} are used in various asymmetric syntheses. Examples include [[Diels-Alder reaction]]s,<ref name="Ahrendt Borths MacMillan pp. 4243–4244" /> [[1,3-dipolar cycloaddition]]s,<ref name="Jen Wiener MacMillan pp. 9874–9875">{{cite journal | last1=Jen | first1=Wendy S. | last2=Wiener | first2=John J. M. | last3=MacMillan | first3=David W. C. | title=New Strategies for Organic Catalysis: The First Enantioselective Organocatalytic 1,3-Dipolar Cycloaddition | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | publisher=American Chemical Society (ACS) | volume=122 | issue=40 | date=26 September 2000 | issn=0002-7863 | doi=10.1021/ja005517p | pages=9874–9875| bibcode=2000JAChS.122.9874J | url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20170406-070216339 }}</ref> [[Friedel-Crafts alkylation]]s<ref name="Paras MacMillan pp. 4370–4371">{{cite journal | last1=Paras | first1=Nick A. | last2=MacMillan | first2=David W. C. | title=New Strategies in Organic Catalysis: The First Enantioselective Organocatalytic Friedel−Crafts Alkylation | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | publisher=American Chemical Society (ACS) | volume=123 | issue=18 | date=13 April 2001 | issn=0002-7863 | doi=10.1021/ja015717g | pages=4370–4371| pmid=11457218 | bibcode=2001JAChS.123.4370P | url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechAUTHORS:20170411-120017472 }}</ref> or [[Michael addition]]s.<ref name="Paras MacMillan pp. 7894–7895" />

MacMillan has also extensively developed photoredox catalysis for use in organic synthesis.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Prier|first1=Christopher K.|last2=Rankic|first2=Danica A.|last3=MacMillan|first3=David W. C.|date=2013-03-19|title=Visible Light Photoredox Catalysis with Transition Metal Complexes: Applications in Organic Synthesis|journal=Chemical Reviews|volume=113|issue=7|pages=5322–5363|doi=10.1021/cr300503r|issn=0009-2665|pmc=4028850|pmid=23509883}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shaw|first1=Megan H.|last2=Twilton|first2=Jack|last3=MacMillan|first3=David W. C.|date=2016-08-19|title=Photoredox Catalysis in Organic Chemistry|url=https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.joc.6b01449|journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry|volume=81|issue=16|pages=6898–6926|doi=10.1021/acs.joc.6b01449|issn=0022-3263|pmc=4994065|pmid=27477076}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nicewicz|first1=David A.|last2=MacMillan|first2=David W. C.|date=2008-10-03|title=Merging Photoredox Catalysis with Organocatalysis: The Direct Asymmetric Alkylation of Aldehydes|journal=Science|volume=322|issue=5898|pages=77–80|doi=10.1126/science.1161976|pmc=2723798|pmid=18772399|bibcode=2008Sci...322...77N }}</ref>

In the early 2020s, MacMillan expanded his research into chemical biology, including the development of µMap, a photocatalytic proximity-labeling platform that enables the mapping of molecular interactions at nanometer-scale resolution.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Geri |first1=Jacob B. |last2=Oakley |first2=James V. |last3=Reyes-Robles |first3=Tamara |last4=Wang |first4=Tao |last5=McCarver |first5=Stefan J. |last6=White |first6=Cory H. |last7=Rodriguez-Rivera |first7=Frances P. |last8=Parker |first8=Dann L. |last9=Hett |first9=Erik C. |last10=Fadeyi |first10=Olugbeminiyi O. |last11=Oslund |first11=Rob C. |last12=MacMillan |first12=David W. C. |title=Microenvironment mapping via Dexter energy transfer on immune cells |journal=Science |volume=367 |issue=6482 |pages=1091–1097 |date=6 March 2020 |doi=10.1126/science.aay4106 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aay4106|pmc=7336666 }}</ref> The technology subsequently became a focus of his laboratory's research into biological systems, including cancer biology, and in 2025 he was appointed a Distinguished Scholar of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research.<ref name=DistinguishedScholar />

Between 2010 and 2014, MacMillan was the founding editor-in-chief of the journal ''[[Chemical Science (journal)|Chemical Science]]'', the flagship general chemistry journal published by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name=nas />

{{As of| March 2024}}, MacMillan has an [[h-index]] of 125 according to [[Google Scholar]]<ref>{{Google Scholar id}}</ref> and of 115 according to [[Scopus]].<ref>{{Scopus id|7102854006}}</ref>
